newsitem.title: UK: Volatility leaves commodities, direction uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Volatility leaves commodities, direction uncertain.

text.p: Volatility went out of world commodity markets on Wednesday with prices barely moving in many raw materials and in the agricultural spectrum.
Dealers searched for fresh short term direction during a sluggish day's trade.
On the industrial metals market, prices for all London Metal Exchange (LME) contracts were flat.
Flagship copper led the complex higher early on covering of short positions and expectations of LME stock declines later in the week, but bank selling soon emerged to cap the rally.
Aluminium, the second most heavily traded of the LME metals, also edged higher early on Wednesday before surrendering gains.
Benchmark three month copper futures ended the afternoon at $1,922 a tonne, up $2. Aluminium was unchanged at $1,400, just $13 above this week's 2-1/4 year lows.
Floor traders said near term direction for copper was unclear, with influential selling expected to emerge in strength but buying interest for LME copper stocks picking up.
"The market is tightening up. There has been a lot of physical business going on during the last 24 hours, and copper stocks should show another good drawdown (on Friday)," one said.
On the soft commodity markets, coffee, sugar and cocoa futures all took their lead from New York.
November robusta coffee futures gained $20 to $1,524 a tonne while benchmark December cocoa futures rose nine stg to 994.
At 1640 GMT December white sugar was up $0.90 to $328.50.
On the precious metals market gold prices enjoyed a brief rally early in a delayed reaction to the surprise U.S. decision to leave interest rates unchanged.
A rise would have increased the holding costs of gold, making it less alluring to the investor.
But renewed concerns about the proposed IMF gold sale capped the rally later in the day. In Europe gold closed 60 cents firmer at $382.40/$382.90 per ounce.
The rare platinum group metal rhodium was under severe pressure from speculative selling during the last week.

It was quoted at around $245 an ounce on Wednesday, a far cry from the dizzy heights of $7,000 reached in 1990 as booming demand from its main user the autocatalyst industry burnt off global supplies.
Traders said rhodium could drop to $200 before buying emerged.
In the Chicago grain pit, corn futures firmed at midsession as traders mulled delays in harvesting the U.S. crop due to expectations of wet weather this week in key growing regions.
At 1625 GMT corn was 1/2 to 1-1/4 cents per bushel higher, with December up 1/2 cent at $3.11.
